title: Ivy Anderson's personality on stage
summary: Cootie says Ivy was better in person than on records; Dance discusses her Oriental Theater debut and Duke's liking for singers.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them

blocks.x: I wonder -- you see, Ivy must have been in the band then. That wasn't made without a vocal, was it?
I don't think so.
I don't think so. I think Ivy must have been in the band. Would you -- does that seem right to you in 1932?
I don't remember the year.
I'll tell you why. Because later on in '32, in May of '32, there's "Stormy Weather", and Ivy certainly made that. Remember?
Yeah.
So she must have come in the band. While we're on that subject, you must have some -- you must remember Ivy coming in the band.
No, I don't remember what year she came in the band.
No. But you remember the Ori -- that she opened up at the Oriental theater.
Yeah. At the Oriental Theater. Yeah.
And she was scared, wasn't she?
I don't remember that.
You don't. Well, she told me that she --
Because I didn't know her then.
No.
We didn't have time to be thinking about nobody else.
(Laughter)
Everybody was all wrapped up with what they were doing.
Yeah.
On their horns.
Uh-huh.
Yeah. Well, I mean it was something, because you know, you'd never had a girl singer in the band before.
No.

And of course -- of course, Duke had a big thing about singers, didn't he? I mean, he really did love -- he loved singers, didn't he? I mean, all through his entire career he was always turning up singers.
Yeah. He --
Don't you think he did?
Yeah. He came up with, you know, singers. He liked singers, yeah.

I mean, I don't say -- I'm not saying that they're singers that you would maybe be turning up yourself. Or I mean, now Earl Hines has a thing about singers. He's turned up a number of singers. He turned up Billy Eckstine, and he turned up Sarah Vaughan, he turned up Madeleine Greene, you know, and a number of people. But with him, his thing was more, you know, legit, or more qualified singers, if I can say that. Duke had a thing about singers with a style, didn't he? That offered something. Well, because, like Hibler had his own style. Who was that boy in the -- a nice singer -- that boy at the time of "Jump for Joy". What's his name? The first boy singer, remember? A good looking boy.
Herb Jeffries?
Yeah. Herb Jeffries.
Yeah. He was very good.
He was good.
I liked him.
I did, too, yeah. He was a good singer. But not -- but nothing flashy.
No.

Or sensational. But he was a good singer. But I mean if Ivy hadn't -- if they hadn't, Duke or Sunny, if they hadn't worked up an act for Ivy, she'd have never gone over so big. To my way of thinking. What do you think?
Well, she had a lot of personality.
Yeah.
Herself. And while -- I don't think that Ivy was -- what would you say, now? A good singer on records, or vocalist. I think she was much better in person.
Yeah. Right. Right. She came across in person.
Yeah. She came across. She could put over a song.
Yeah.
Right. That's what I liked about Ivy.
Well, I mean, because actually, while Ivy
did justice to her numbers, she didn't have the beautiful voice that some singers have, you know.
No.
She didn't have the same equipment to bring that some singers did.
That's right.

And of course -- I mean, her background, before she came into the band, she was a soubrette, you know, which is sort of -- she stayed in character that way, really, didn't she? I mean, like you know, when Duke would bring her on -- well, maybe she'd do her "Stormy Weather" and things, but she would always end up with something like -- well, even later on, when Rex would do the funny -- there was always something a little gay, a little funny, a little -- to involve the audience.
Oh, yeah.

Yeah. Incidentally, though, there were -- I don't know what you would say, but I had one or two numbers of hers that I liked very much. One was "I'm Satisfied". Maybe you don't remember it, because you wouldn't play the records the same way we would, you know.
No.
But I've got it written here, somewhere. She did "And No Greater Love". And "Isn't Love the Strangest Thing". She had three or four numbers that were very, very nice, that
she just sang. They were straight numbers. They probably weren't so big on stage. He may not have even used them on stage. But they were good records. You don't remember that "I'm Satisfied"?
No, I don't remember it.
